claims.text: A hybrid computational framework can explicitly decouple lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Incorporating realistic atomistic disorder and defects will improve thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy.
The proposed framework will predict temperature-dependent thermal conductivity within ±10% of experiment.
Previous perfect-crystal-based models have errors of approximately ±30%.
Near-perfect, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystals represent the samples relevant to the low-temperature studies.
Defect-rich HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen represents the high-temperature condition.
The intervention integrates DFT, Green–Kubo, and Boltzmann transport approaches.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
The high-temperature prediction regime is 300–1200 K and includes samples containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Atomic-scale disorder and oxygen-containing defect structures modify vibrational heat transport.
Atomic-scale disorder and oxygen-containing defect structures modify electronic heat transport.
Non-ideal atomic environments and defects induce scattering that the hybrid framework can explicitly account for.
Explicitly accounting for disorder and defect scattering enables separate computation of lattice and electronic heat transport.
Previous analytical approaches relevant to this problem assumed defect-free crystals.
The method will accurately reproduce distinct lattice and electronic contributions in both specified temperature regimes.
The proposed applicability extends to HfNbTaTiZr and similar refractory high-entropy alloys up to 1200 K.
Changes in defect chemistry and sample-to-sample variation may affect the claimed accuracy margin.
Validation will compare controlled near-perfect and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr samples in low- and high-temperature regimes.
The experiment will measure total conductivity, separated lattice and electronic contributions, and defect or impurity levels.
The hypothesis is falsified if prediction errors exceed ±10% across the specified regimes or if the method fails to decouple the two transport contributions relative to the traditional baseline.
